title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation, and the synthetic part of it is the likeness of a named public official presented on a video call. The fraud did not depend on a model getting a fact wrong. It depended on the victim treating a generated face as the person it claimed to be, and on a second claim of authority from someone described as a CBI officer. Two identities were asserted, one of them fabricated visually.

The failure sits at the consumer messaging layer, where a call arrives carrying no verified connection to the person it appears to show. Nothing in the call distinguished the generated likeness from the official it depicted, and the payment requests were made inside that same conversation. Catching it would have required confirming the offer through a channel independent of the caller, or a platform ability to flag a synthetic caller, and the reporting does not describe either being present.

What is not established is who produced the deepfake, or whether any detection was attempted before or during the call. The account rests on one complaint to police and a case registered under the Information Technology Act, which is not a finding of guilt against any identified person.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29 year old Bengaluru security guard, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on September 9. The caller used an AI generated deepfake of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay and claimed to offer financial aid. The fraudster promised Rs 11 lakh and said a manager would arrange a transfer from a foreign account in dollars. This is the first such case reported in the city.

Giri was told Rs 5 lakh was allotted, then asked to pay Rs 5,000 as exchange charges. Later he paid Rs 18,000 after being told his PIN was locked. A person claiming to be CBI officer Thakur demanded over Rs 50,000 as a fine, and Giri made more payments totaling over Rs 1.04 lakh. When another Rs 50,000 was demanded, he refused and realized he had been duped. He contacted cybercrime helpline 1930 and Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act, and police urged people not to trust such calls or make payments.
